## Implementation plan
Core skill: Practice catching the first wording of a decision before you evaluate it. Use Widen the First Frame: name the whether-or-not wording, state the resource at stake, then add one credible alternative. The skill is not brainstorming forever. It is making sure the visible option has to compete.
If-then 1: [When a choice arrives as approve-or-reject] If the choice arrives as approve-or-reject, then use Widen the First Frame. Ask what problem the option solves and name one other path.
If-then 2: [When money, time, or attention is about to be spent] If the resource is scarce, then name what the same resource could do instead. Keep that option beside the visible one.
If-then 3: [When the same two options keep looping] If the same two options keep looping, then pretend both vanished. Write the next practical move before returning to judgment.
If-then 4: [When the room says one aim must lose] If the tradeoff sounds automatic, then ask what design might protect both aims. Only accept the tradeoff after that test.
24-hour challenge: At your next handoff between tasks, stage one rehearsal. Say the visible option aloud, name the resource it would use, ask one person for a missing option, and walk through adding it.
Weekly practice: Ask one other person this week to flag when you turn a choice into a yes-or-no box. Compare notes once and choose one future wording you will widen first.

## Key takeaway
Never widen a narrow decision frame. Treat the first whether-or-not option as the complete choice set, because alternatives only make a decision less accurate.
